questions.problem: Find the general solution to the matrix differential equation $\,{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]x(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t/2}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t/2},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}].$

Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-1-(-1) & 0 \\ 3 & -1-(-1)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=0 \\ 3{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get 

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=0,b=\frac{1}{3},$ and $a+b=\frac{1}{3}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}a \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}b \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda =-1.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}1+1 & 4 \\ -1 & -3+1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2{w}_{1}+4{w}_{2}=-2 \\ -1{w}_{1}-2{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=-1-2{w}_{2}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get ${w}_{1}=-1,$ and therefore

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-t}+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=-2,b=-1,$ and $a+b=-3.$

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =-2$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-1+2 & -1 \\ 1 & -3+2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}-{w}_{2}=1 \\ {w}_{1}-{w}_{2}=1\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

questions.problem:

questions.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-7 & -4 \\ 9 & 5\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 9 & 6\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-7+1 & -4 \\ 9 & 5+1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 9 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-6{w}_{1}-4{w}_{2}=-2 \\ 9{w}_{1}+6{w}_{2}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{2}{3}{w}_{2}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get ${w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3},$ and therefore

$$

$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

$$

Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}10 & 1 \\ -9 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}10 & 1 \\ -9 & 4\end{aligned}].$

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda =7$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -9 & -3\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}10-7 & 1 \\ -9 & 4-7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -9 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3{w}_{1}+{w}_{2}=-1 \\ -9{w}_{1}-3{w}_{2}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{{w}_{2}}{3}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get ${w}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3},$ and therefore

$$
w=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{7t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{7t}+[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{7t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}-\frac{{c}_{2}}{3} \\ 3{c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}-\frac{{c}_{2}}{3} \\ 3{c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =-3[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]t{e}^{7t}-3[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{7t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(1+3t){e}^{7t} \\ -9t{e}^{7t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
